sets how close the calling actor's move must come to stop: 0x0034A9F0 -> 0x0026B450 stores the reach at steering record +0x20 for a class-3 actor, and the move 0x002E45E0 stops when the actor is within it of its target point, adding both bodies' radii for an actor target (Movement-And-Pathfinding/facing-and-steering.md)

unbinds every camera shot of the calling script's manager: 0x00351540 -> 0x003DA000 resets side A of its camera entry tables, the lookups +0x18 and +0x1A to -1 and each of the four entries' +0x08 to 0 and +0x0A to -1, so no shot of the script's camera-shot table stays bound (Graphics/scripted-camera.md)

binds camera shot n of the calling script's camera-shot table to camera entry 0 to 3 and shows it in the given frame: 0x0034F2F0 -> 0x003DA400(slot, record, 0.0, entry, frame) refuses an entry above 3, a null table [slot + 0xD8] or a record past its count, and otherwise fills entry +0x110 + entry x 0x18 (clock 0.0, the record, rate 1.0), initialises the camera driver block (0x00257230) and publishes the entry in the frame word (0 the main frame +0x18, 1 the sub frame +0x1A)

starts shot s of the calling script's camera-shot table on camera channel c (0-3) from its first frame: 0x0034F930 is camerastart_7d with frame -1 (0x003DA400(slot, shot, 0.0, channel, -1)), which fills the channel entry, loads the shot into the camera driver block (0x00257230) and publishes the channel in word +0x18 of the slot; a channel above 3, a missing shot table or a shot past its count is refused

stops the calling actor's move or move-to-actor where it stands: 0x0034D8F0 -> 0x0026AE90(actor, 0) stores steering mode 0, clears actor byte +0x0D bit 0x10, cancels the steer (0x002E55C0: movement mode 2 torn down, speed and context +0xD0 zeroed) and zeroes +0x7C (Movement-And-Pathfinding/facing-and-steering.md)

stops the calling actor's turn, timed turn or move where it is: 0x0034DC60 -> 0x0026C120(actor, 0) stores movement mode 0 at steering record +0x28; with the turn lock +0x65 set it also clears the steer channel (0x002EBE50(actor, 0, 0)) and pushes the flags to the render record (0x002E8EE0), then 0x002E6300 runs; nothing for an actor that is not a character (byte +0x03 and 0xE0 other than 0x60)

opens message window slot n with the line of the given text id at the given corner, with an automatic size and the given style: 0x0034A090 pushes 0 as the window kind and runs mes 0x00348DF0, then 0x002E1EA0 sets the style, 0x002E1F80 the corner and 0x002E1F40 the kind; a kind-0 window opens and closes at once, without the opening and closing runs (0x002E177E; Story-Events-And-Hunts/script-language-differences.md, Menus-And-HUD/message-windows.md)

makes the calling actor collide with other characters (non-zero) or pass through them (0): 0x0034D120 -> 0x0026A430 sets actor byte +0x08 bit 0x8, which makes it an active body for the movement and battle obstruction tests (0x002EA7F0, 0x003357B0), and +0x09 bit 0x40, which puts its placement in the frame list the camera eye lift walks (0x002E6330, 0x0046DB50)

sets the calling actor's push weight to n: 0x0034DEA0 converts it to a float (0x0034DEBD) and 0x0026DAC0 stores it at the secondary context [actor+0xC0] +0x148 (0x0026DACC), then copies that to the body's weight [[actor+0xC0]+0x138] +8 (0x0026DAE0-0x0026DAFE); with no secondary context nothing is stored. The weight decides who yields when two bodies overlap (0x00314E10: a zero weight against a positive one takes all the separation, a negative weight a share of 0 so the overlap never moves it); 0x0025B470 then keeps only bit 0x10 of the body's mask word +0x110 and sets that bit for a negative weight outside a town (Movement-And-Pathfinding/movement-bodies-and-separation.md)

closes the screen in with the mask's two bands and hides the HUD: 0x00353D90 pops the argument and drops it, then 0x002E2440(0, 0), or the fast open 0x002E2440(1, 0) and 0x002E1C70(1, 3) while the issuer's manager is skipping (0x00267310); 0x002E2440 opens the bands (0x0029D290: widgets [0x0209C380] and [0x0209C318]), raises time-stop request 16 (0x002274E0), sets row 4 of the action table (0x0215F1D0 bits 0x100203), stops the map wind on model bones (0x00267D40(1, 1)) and sets 0x0215F1B2 = 1, and 0x002E1C40(0, 3) sets bit 0x8 of the HUD hide word 0x0215F1AC

plays music track n from the beginning at full volume: the begin 0x00342770 loads it into a track slot when no slot holds it (0x00360C20, 0x00361630) unless the manager is skipping, the poll 0x00341F90 holds while that slot is loading, and the result 0x00342F80 starts it through 0x002DECE0 (volume 0x0215EF4D = 0x7F, resume point cleared 0x001DBC10, started 0x001DBBD0, current at 0x0215EF44) unless it is already the current track (0x002DEC00); while skipping it records the track for the skip end (0x00360960; Sound-And-Music/music-table.md)

The moment a character or an enemy locks in an action - from the menu, a gambit, its AI, an automatic attack or the next hit of a combo - the game records what it is doing and to whom. Nothing about damage, cost or timing is decided at that moment.
cause: Action commit: locking in an action and target, the leader's target, the attacker mask and the idle-unit queue

phenomenon: Every command that does something in battle is one row of one table: Attack, each magick and technick, each item use, each summon, Quickening and Concurrence, each Foecraft move, and the traps. The row decides what the action costs, how long it charges, how far it reaches, what it can target, how wide its area is, how strong it is, its element, the statuses it inflicts and where it sits in the command list. The name and help text are in the text banks, and the row holds their ids.
cause: Action definition row: power, targeting, range, element and flag fields of a battle action

phenomenon: After a unit commits to an action, the action runs through a fixed sequence of phases, one or more per frame.
cause: Action phases: delay, charge time, approach, execution and the end of a battle action

phenomenon: When a character or an enemy starts an action, it works out three distances to its target, not one range: reach - further than this and it cannot act;
cause: Action range: near, middle and reach distances and how a unit closes in on its target

phenomenon: When a character or an enemy starts an action, it works out three distances to its target, not one range: middle - the distance it settles at;
cause: Action range: near, middle and reach distances and how a unit closes in on its target

phenomenon: When a character or an enemy starts an action, it works out three distances to its target, not one range: near - closer than this and it may step back.
cause: Action range: near, middle and reach distances and how a unit closes in on its target

phenomenon: When an action hits, its whole outcome is first written into one record - damage or healing for the target and the user, statuses to add or remove, items stolen or poached, levels gained, stat changes on an enemy, gil spent - and then applied in one pass, in a fixed order. A field left at its "empty" value is simply skipped, so each action only touches what it actually changes. Levels are applied before the statuses, statuses before HP and MP, and the gil change comes last. When the target cannot be affected at that moment, nothing in the record is applied.
cause: Action results: the result record a resolved action produces and how it is applied to target and user

phenomenon: The player, a gambit or an enemy's AI picks one target. Everyone else the action hits is gathered later, when the action's state machine reaches its target step, from where everybody stands at that moment.
cause: Area of effect: radius, cone and line targeting, which side an area hits, and the target list

phenomenon: The battle log shows short lines about what just happened: a technick that failed and why, a poach, an item used on a party member, a status cured, a steal, a level gained. Each line is one row of the battle message table (Battle message list).
cause: Battle log: which result posts which battle message, the repeat limit and the 24-unit visibility rule

phenomenon: A boss or story fight is not marked by one setting. The area's script builds it from separate pieces: The boss is an enemy in a numbered group. Ordinary enemies are in group 0. When every member of a group has been defeated, the game locks the controls, freezes the battle and, for groups set up for it, records the group number where the area's script can read it.
cause: Boss fights: enemy groups, the group-defeated signal, the battle freeze, the exit lock and the boss gauge

phenomenon: A boss or story fight is not marked by one setting. phenomenon: When an area or a scene loads, its characters and objects appear, run their scripts and react; in battle they fight. When the party leaves the area or the scene ends, they all disappear together.
cause: Actor lifecycle: an actor record from its manager's bind to the release, and when its handle stops working

phenomenon: Everything that moves or talks in a field belongs to one of five managers. The first one owns the field itself: its townspeople, doors, pots and triggers, the party and the music. The others hold the actors a cutscene or an event brings in, so that a scene can load its own cast without touching the field's. Loading a field or a scene binds a script file to a manager, carves out the records for its actors, and from then on the per-frame pass drives those actors through that manager (field runtime).
cause: Actor managers: the five manager slots at 0x02098E10, their bind, their record pool, their variable homes and their camera entry tables

phenomenon: When a character joins, leaves or changes job, or a battle starts, each party member briefly vanishes, its model, held items and body are swapped for the ones its current definition calls for, and it reappears in place. A scene waits while `partyallread` runs. The frames the member is invisible are the loads this machine waits on.
cause: Actor model rebuild: the state machine that reloads an actor's model, attachments and body for its current definition, and what runs it

phenomenon: Every townsperson, door, trigger line, party member and monster in a field is one record owned by one of the five actor managers. When a field or a scene loads, the manager's script payload says how many actors of each kind it brings, the records are carved out of one block, and each is set up with its script entry, its position and steering state and its slots for resource requests and waits. The record stays alive until the manager unloads, when the block is freed.
cause: Actor record: the record every field actor is driven through, its pool, its classes, its sub-objects and its lifetime

phenomenon: A battle unit becomes something when a definition is applied to it: Vaan with his level, equipment, licences and gambits, or a Wolf with its stats, its one weapon and its loot flags. Party members come from one authored table and enemies from the area's enemy table, and every piece of combat code can tell the two apart by one byte in the unit's stats record. A narrower split of the party side, by the type number, decides who earns experience and licence points and who is only a guest or a summoned creature.
cause: Battle unit construction: the party and enemy definition tables, the stats record a unit gets, the kind byte and the type partition

phenomenon: Everything that can take part in a battle, the party, guests and every enemy on the field, occupies one of thirty-two combat slots. When the slots are all taken, the next thing that would join a fight simply does not: it stands there without a unit, with no message and no error. Separately, a small class field on every actor decides what the engine may do with it: a steerable character can be moved and positioned, a placed object such as a door has a position but ignores movement, and a trigger line can be given its six coordinates by a script.
cause: Battle units: the pool of combat slots, who gets one, the actor class bits, the handle and the flag word

phenomenon: Every actor in a field runs a small script: the townspeople, the doors, the treasure pots, the cutscene triggers, the party members themselves. Each frame the game visits every actor once and gives its script a turn, unless the script is waiting for something, such as a line of dialogue to close, a walk to finish or another actor to reach a point.
cause: Field runtime: how a frame drives every actor's script through the manager slots and the wait slots

phenomenon: A townsperson's name tag reads "Imperial", "Rabanastran" or "Wistful Bangaa" until the player has spoken to that person or a script reveals them, after which the same person is "Sherral" or "Arryl". Nothing about the character changes: every field character carries a name number, the number picks a pair of names from one file, and a story flag with the same number decides which of the two is shown. Most pairs repeat the same name twice, so for them the flag changes nothing visible.
cause: NPC names: the npcdic.bin name pairs, the actor's name id, and the story flag that swaps a name

phenomenon: The status screen, the party menu and the HUD name strip show a member's name, level, HP and its cap, MP and its bars, experience and the points to the next level, LP, the equipment, the status icons with their countdowns, and whether the member is the leader, KO'd, engaged, out of range or in the middle of an action. None of those screens reads the party's stats directly: each asks for a fresh 192-byte snapshot of the member and reads that.
cause: Party member status record: the snapshot the menus and HUD read a party member through, field by field

phenomenon: Nothing, in normal play. When a C++ exception passes through a function, small compiler-written routines destroy that function's half-built objects, and a catch routine decides where the game carries on. None of them shows a message box.
cause: Exception handling: x64 unwind data, funclets and the C++ EH tables

phenomenon: Nothing in normal play. The executable does not ask for address randomisation, so Windows loads it at `0x00120000`, and an address in this database is the address in the running game unless mandatory ASLR (Exploit Protection's "Force randomization for images", `ForceRelocateImages`), switched on for the system or for the game, loads it elsewhere: the image ships its relocations, so that setting can move it.
cause: Image hardening: the executable's load address, DEP, Control Flow Guard and stack cookies as built

phenomenon: Much of the engine's type information and many of its singletons do not exist when the game starts; each is built the first time code asks for it, often during a load. If something stops a thread in the middle of such a first build without letting it finish or unwind, every later thread that needs the same object waits forever: the game sits on a loading screen using little CPU and does not crash. That outcome follows from the code below.
cause: Lazy statics and one-time initialisation: thread-safe local statics, their guards, the shared lock and the release on exceptions

phenomenon: Smooth movement and sound. A character turning to face a target eases in: the turn is slow when it is nearly facing the right way and full speed from 60 degrees off. Range tests measure across the ground and ignore height. Positional sound works out the direction and distance of each source with four-wide vector code. Almost every sine, cosine, square root and power in the game is worked out by the C runtime that Windows provides, not by code inside the executable.
cause: Maths library: the C runtime maths imports, the inline SSE maths and the floating-point setup

phenomenon: The game's memory use in Task Manager climbs as areas, models and movies load and falls as they are released. About 257 MiB is taken in one go at start-up for the resource arenas. The RAM file cache may grow to a third of the machine's physical memory, never below 32 MiB and never above 4 GiB, and on start the game raises its own process priority and widens its working set to nearly all physical memory.
cause: Memory and allocation: the C runtime heap, the game's allocation wrappers, new and delete, aligned blocks and the subsystem allocators

phenomenon: Nothing directly. The game's own code keeps its strings, vectors, sets and maps in EASTL (see EASTL strings and containers). The Microsoft containers on this page belong to code built against the standard library instead: the post-effect library keeps three lookup maps and parses its licence into a fourth, one start-up initialiser builds a static map, and one event-path check uses `std::regex`.
cause: MSVC containers: the std::map tree, std::string and std::regex code linked into the executable

phenomenon: Nothing directly. Every character, effect, sound object and menu element is built and freed through these few patterns, and a hook that breaks one of them shows up as a crash or a slow leak when objects are created or destroyed, typically on area changes.
cause: Object construction and destruction: vtable installs, deleting destructors, deallocators and owned buffers

phenomenon: When the game crashes it writes a memory dump next to itself or into its working folder and shows a box titled `error` that reads "Fatal error encountered." (the text exists in all nine of the executable's resource languages). Nothing else here is visible: the sound and post-effect libraries still write diagnostic text to the Windows debug channel, which only a debug viewer shows.
cause: Runtime services: what the game asks Windows and the C runtime for, its crash dumps, threads and debug output

phenomenon: Nothing directly: this runs between launching the game and its first window. It decides what exists when: every global object below exists before the game's own code starts, and none of their teardowns runs when the player quits from the menu.

phenomenon: What a mistake in the file does depends on the mistake: - a code used for two controls, a reserved code, or a control of the first set left empty or out of range: the whole file is ignored and the default controls are used; - a line that is neither a `[KeyboardN]` header nor a `name=value` binding: reading stops there and the lines before it are kept, unless the first set is then incomplete, which makes the game ignore the whole file; - a value or set number that is not a number, or is too large: the game stops; - a line of 128 characters or more: its first 127 are read as a line and the rest is left unread. If that part is a binding or a header that parses, the game hangs while it starts, reading the file forever; otherwise it is treated like any other line of its kind; - a set number other than 1-3: its bindings are written outside the three sets, over other data; - a control name longer than 64 characters: the game stops.

phenomenon: The characters, monsters, treasure chests, gadgets and weapons a zone or event script brings on screen. When a script binds a model to an actor it usually names the model by its position in this table, so the table decides which body, chest or prop appears. A wrong entry puts a different model in the scene; a missing one gives the bind no model.
cause: Actor manifest: the script section that lists the models its bind verbs name by position

phenomenon: When a summon lands, a blade rings off stone or the ground shudders in a cutscene, the camera jolts and trembles for a set time and then settles. Each tremble is an authored shake in the scene's section 11, with working names such as `シェイク01`, `振動02` and `手ブレ01`; section 10 is the list of rows the script's shake verbs pick from. The motion is random within authored limits, so the same shake never moves the view twice in exactly the same way.
cause: EBP camera shake: the CML1 shake list and the SHK1 curves that make a scripted camera tremble

phenomenon: The directed camera of a cutscene, and of a field map that frames a moment such as a door opening, is authored as named shots: where the camera starts, where it looks, how it swings or cranes to the next pose and how long that takes. Section 9 holds the shots and section 8 the list of rows a script's camera verbs pick from. 296 of the 345 event scripts and 127 of the 769 field map scripts in a language tree carry them; a map without them keeps the ordinary follow camera.
cause: EBP camera tables: the CML1 shot list and the CAM7 shots a script's camera verbs play

phenomenon: The lamps, fires and coloured fill lights of a cutscene, and the lights a scene switches on and off as it plays. Each record is one light that tints the characters and objects near it; the chunk tables decide which records are lit at a given moment. Field maps carry the same format in their map pack (map pack, slot 17), bound into group 0.
cause: LGT2 light sets: the 0x70-byte light records and chunk tables of an event script's lighting, how they are bound into a light group and how the renderer picks them

phenomenon: The markers the minimap shows during play are listed in the field map script's section 4. Each icon names an object of the zone, and the minimap draws the icon where that object stands, once the icon's story gate passes. The same block lets a script move an actor onto the object an icon names.
cause: EBP navigation icons: the NAVIICN2 block a field map script carries for its minimap markers

phenomenon: Where monsters appear and roam in a zone. A monster spawns at an authored point or at a random spot inside an authored box or ellipse, wanders around a numbered point, and an enemy's gambits can test its distance from one. Scripts read the same points to place actors. None of it is drawn; the entries are why monsters gather in particular parts of a field.
cause: Position entries (FF12POS3): a zone's authored points, boxes and ellipses, the accessor that copies them and the systems that read them

phenomenon: Everything a map does beyond its scenery comes from one `.ebp` file: the people who walk and talk, the doors, chests and save crystals, the weather, the camera cuts and lighting of a cutscene, the signs on the map. Each zone has one, each event has one, and entering a zone or starting an event loads it. The container is the file's table of contents: it says which of these parts a given zone or event carries and where each one starts.
cause: EBP script container: the twenty-slot directory of every zone and event script, and the walk that hands each section to its loader

phenomenon: The script image is the code of a zone or a cutscene: who stands where, what each person says when spoken to, which door opens, how a cutscene's characters move on cue. Each actor in a scene has its own entry in the image with a set of named functions (`init`, `main`, `talk` and so on), and the script interpreter runs those functions a few instructions at a time each frame.
cause: EBP script image: the section-0 header, actor directory, function and jump tables and actor lists a zone or event script runs from

phenomenon: Every line a zone or a cutscene says comes from its script's section 2: what an NPC says when spoken to, a Save Crystal's prompt, a Moogle's yes-or-no question, a Way Stone's list of destinations and the subtitles of a scene. Section 3 holds short captions such as `Ancient Door`, `Way Stone` and `Exit`, which become the name tag of the object the player stands next to. The script holds no text itself, only numbers: renumbering a bank changes what every speaker in the zone says without touching the bytecode.
cause: EBP text sections: the message bank and the field-sign caption bank a script's text ids index

phenomenon: Kill a wandering monster and, after a while, it is back. How long "a while" is belongs to the monster: each one carries a cooldown in whole seconds, rolled once from a base and a range the zone script authored, and measured on a clock that only runs while the field runs. Some monsters can only die so many times per visit; after that number they stay gone until the area forgets them.
cause: Enemy respawning: death counts, cooldowns, the group table that wakes a zone script, and the two-area memory

phenomenon: Monsters appear around you, not on top of you, and usually ahead of you. A zone script asks the engine for a spot: a random distance in a band around the party leader, at a random angle inside an arc centred on the way the leader faces. The default band is 39 to 42 units and the arc a forward half-circle, but almost every zone that cares replaces the band with something much tighter, 5 to 12 units being the commonest, so monsters in those zones appear close.
cause: Enemy spawning: the spawn table, how a zone picks where a monster appears, the ground height, and when it vanishes out of range

phenomenon: Nothing. The names are a trace the compiler left for the C++ `dynamic_cast` and `typeid` operators: every class with virtual functions keeps a record beside its vtable that spells out its own name and its base classes. The game never prints them. They matter because they turn a block of anonymous functions into the methods of a named engine class, and because they show where the game's own code is object-oriented and where it is not.
cause: Class hierarchy: the C++ classes the executable names through RTTI and what they are

phenomenon: Nothing. The shipped game still carries its developers' logging: engine code formats messages such as `[FileCache] …` on every load, and the boot prints the name of each step it runs. None of it reaches the screen. The only cost a player pays is time: each message is still written out in full, up to 16 KB, before it is thrown away unread.
cause: Debug logging: the log call, its sink and the console prints the shipped game still runs

phenomenon: Nothing, in a retail game. The remaster carries the developers' tuning menu: fifteen pages of rows such as "Invincible", "Set gill to max", "Shadow Level", "Water Fresnel Factor" and "Enable 100% successful steal", each a name with a value beside it that a press of left or right would step. The code that draws it and the code that runs every row are in the shipped game, but the byte that opens the menu is never set, so no button sequence shows it.
cause: Debug menu: the developer console object, its fifteen pages, its command dispatcher and the retail rows that still reach it

phenomenon: Press R2 in the field; once the arming counter has run, the word FLEEING appears on the HUD: the party stops answering the enemy, combos stop chaining for anyone who is not Confused or Berserk, and most battle commands are refused until the party fights again. Press R2 again and the label is gone and the party fights. The ordinary state is the fighting one. Area scripts put the party into the fleeing state at map entry and after a teleport, and the game restores the toggle's own state a moment later.
cause: Force fight mode: the flag behind the fleeing state, who sets it and what fleeing changes

phenomenon: Every frame the pad is read, the world is simulated a whole number of steps, the camera follows, sound is mixed, the picture is drawn and the loop waits for the next tick. In ordinary field play every frame runs exactly one step, at 30 and at 60 frames per second alike; at 60 the frame waits one tick instead of two.
cause: Frame update order: what runs each frame for the field, the battle layer and every unit

phenomenon: The moment the game finds its data. Everything a player ever sees comes through one archive, `FFXII_TZA.vbf`, opened once at start by the application object; a few steps later one byte is set that the rest of the application waits on. Before it is set the window exists but nothing runs; after it, every frame goes through the same tick: the managers are pumped in a fixed order, the game's own state machine advances, the screen fade is stepped, and the frame ends.
cause: Game application object: the root object, its vtable and the boot order

phenomenon: The remaster draws things the PlayStation 2 original could not: depth of field that blurs the background, ambient occlusion in corners, image-based lighting on skin and metal, cascaded shadows, water with reflection and refraction, and a post-processing pass over the whole frame. The options menu can switch several of them on or off or pick a quality level (game settings), but no option has a strength slider.
cause: Graphics settings: the render settings block, its scene-config keys, its defaults and the shader constants it feeds

phenomenon: Every list the menus draw, the Items tab with its quantities, the Loot tab, the Magicks and Technicks lists, the gambit condition picker, the Key Items tab, the bazaar's goods and the licence board's node names, is built by asking one question of one function: here is an id, tell me its name, its description and how many the party has.
cause: Item and ability ids: the sixteen-bit id space, the fifteen inventory classes, the thirty-two-class validator and the query record

phenomenon: An Esper on the field, a chocobo under the party, a town, and a cutscene that has taken the party over are four states the game keeps apart with one number. While an Esper is out, the summoner is the character the game follows and the Esper holds the fourth place in the party selection. On a chocobo the rider steers the mount and the other members leave the field. In a town the party is never out of play from KO, Stone or X-Zone, and the town's own leader row is followed. During an event the script owns the party: the gambits, the battle menu and the controls stop answering.
cause: Party control modes: the summon, chocobo, town and event-party levels and who may set them

phenomenon: Nothing directly. Every particle that is placed, every bone that is multiplied through a matrix, every vertex that is projected for the old PlayStation 2 style effects, and the search for the sound source nearest the listener all pass through this code. On the PlayStation 2 that work was hand-written assembly for the console's vector unit and its 128-bit integer instructions. The remaster did not rewrite those routines.
cause: PS2 CPU emulation: the in-memory PS2 register set that translated assembly runs on

phenomenon: Particle effects, weapon trails and the other PlayStation 2 era effect drawing look as they did on the console. On the PlayStation 2 that drawing was fed to the second vector unit, VU1, as command packets for its interface, VIF1, and the unit's microprograms wrote primitives for the Graphics Synthesizer.
cause: PS2 VIF1 and VU1 emulation: the packet decoder, the recompiled microprograms and the GS replay

phenomenon: Two launches of the game roll the same numbers until a save is loaded; loading a save reseeds the generator from the system clock, so from then on the two launches roll differently. A player who sets the frame limit to 60 sees every authored duration keep its wall-clock length. Whether Circle or Cross confirms is set at start into two masks every menu reads, and set again when the Config screen's confirm button option changes. The game's whole working memory, a quarter of a gigabyte in eleven blocks, is claimed before the first screen appears.
cause: Startup constants: the random seed, the frame-rate constant, the memory budget and the confirm button mapping

phenomenon: Nothing changes on screen because of this word: it ships with every bit set and nothing in the game clears one. What it describes is the order in which the interface advances each frame: the widgets, the menus, the battle display and the message boxes are sixteen update groups run one after another by one pump, and every group first asks this word whether it may run. A build that cleared a bit would freeze that part of the interface while the rest kept moving.
cause: Subsystem update flags: the enable word that switches the sixteen interface update groups on or off each frame

phenomenon: Open the main menu in the field and everyone stops mid-step. When an action is shown on its own, the rest of the field holds while the acting unit keeps moving. Enter a conversation and the talking actors play while the scene around them waits. Skip a scene and the world resumes cleanly. Each of these is a different request to one registry, and the differences between them, who keeps moving, whether only scripts freeze or animation too, which sound groups mute, come from a small permission record written for each request.
cause: Time stop and freeze: how menus, cutscenes, Stop magicks and skippable scenes halt actors

phenomenon: Which monsters an area can field, how strong each is at each level, what it can steal and drop from, and which gambits it follows all come from the area's `.ard`. Entering a new area swaps the whole set; an area without one has no enemy definitions at all.
cause: Area battle data (.ard and .nmb): the per-area file of enemy definitions, class rows, stat rows, gambit order sets, motion overrides and preloaded models, and its companion

phenomenon: Two kinds of menu picture come out of these files. The item pictures that menu list rows show are 64 x 96 pages of the eight `item_gra` sheets, decoded one at a time when a row needs one. The large character silhouette behind the Gambits screen is one of six groups of pages in `char_silhouette.as7`, picked by the party member being edited.
cause: Menu graphics containers (.as7): the compressed page archives behind item pictures and character silhouettes

phenomenon: The game keeps drawing while it loads. Remastered models, maps, textures, fonts and the text lists that name them, and the PS2-era files the game logic asks for, are mostly read on a separate loading thread, and the code that asked is told on a later run of the completion pump that the data is there. When a summon, a monster or an NPC model is read, the game also reads that model's character effect file and hands both over as one block.
cause: Asynchronous load manager: the loading thread, its request records, the four load kinds and the .efx appendix

phenomenon: Every number the battle system looks up, from an item's price and a spell's power to a character's starting stats, a gambit's target and an enemy's level, comes from a table the game loads once at start-up or each time the party enters a new area. When a table is missing, the game does not fall back to a default: most lookups read from address 0 and the game crashes, and the few that first check an id against the table's count refuse the id instead.
cause: Authored data tables: the 64-slot registry that holds the battle_pack.bin tables, the area .ard tables and the license boards, how each is bound, and how rows are found

phenomenon: Two casts of the same spell never look quite the same: sparks leave at slightly different angles, embers live slightly different times, a glow pulses on its own schedule. Most numbers authored in effect data are not flat values but "this much, give or take that much", or a curve over time, and they are rolled or sampled each time they are used. The roll comes from the presentation generator, so it never touches damage, drops or anything else in play.
cause: Authored expressions: the 16-byte value records in effect data, their operand kinds, curves and six operators, the random spread, and the colour forms

phenomenon: Every ability, item, status, place and monster-family name, every gambit target line and every menu label and help line is a string looked up by number. The battle names live in one block of `battle_pack.bin`, loaded at start-up; the menu and help text lives in separate files that a menu loads when it first needs them.
cause: Battle and menu text tables: the word banks in battle_pack.bin, the st2e string tables behind menu and help text, and how a text id becomes a string

phenomenon: The game's data lives in one 31 GB file, `FFXII_TZA.vbf`, in the game folder beside the `x64` folder that holds the program. It opens at once at start-up, because only its index is read and checked; the data itself is read a piece at a time as the game needs it. An edited index the game does not accept leaves the archive unmounted, and every file the game then asks for fails to open. A compressed block that fails to inflate shows a Windows error box, "Broken game data, please repair or restore the data."
cause: Bigfile archive: the VBF container, how its index loads and is checked, and how a read reaches the file

phenomenon: The game pastes these files into three menu pictures at run time: when a guest is in the party, the guest's portrait `face_guestNN` into `partytop_8_c`;
cause: Bin_menu images: the headerless 8-bit guest portraits and area icons pasted into menu pictures

phenomenon: The game pastes these files into three menu pictures at run time: a guest's small face, one cell of `mini_guest_face`, into `mini_face_c`;
cause: Bin_menu images: the headerless 8-bit guest portraits and area icons pasted into menu pictures

phenomenon: The game pastes these files into three menu pictures at run time: when an area flag is set, the icon `map_efe0N` into `battle_4_c`. Four of these flags are the ones that stop the party using Attack, Magicks, Technicks or Items (command availability).
cause: Bin_menu images: the headerless 8-bit guest portraits and area icons pasted into menu pictures

phenomenon: The staff roll's scrolling text is set in six faces, three typefaces each with a drop-shadow companion. The `.btm` sheets are the PS2-era pixel cells of those faces. A line with a shadow is drawn twice, the shadow face first and the face over it; the quad the remaster puts on screen takes its pixels from the matching `font_stf` font of the font list, and the sheet cell goes into the GS packet path beside it.
cause: ExFont sheets (.btm): the 4-bit glyph cells of the six staff-roll faces, how they are loaded and how a glyph finds its cell

phenomenon: Each character, monster, summon and weapon model has its own footsteps, cries and swing sounds. Those sounds are played by the model's animations (Animation sounds), but the banks they come from are named here: one row per model, giving the sound blocks to load with the model and, for 39 models (14 characters, 11 NPC models, 13 summons and the monster model `m1208`), the bank their battle shouts come from. A model with an empty row loads no sound blocks; background objects, gadgets and treasure chests ship with every row empty.
cause: Character sound tables (chse): the per-model table that names the sound blocks and battle-voice bank a model's animation sounds play from

phenomenon: The colours of the pictures on a location map. No location-map picture uses its own palette: every map takes the third colour table of `clutpack_ys.bin`, except the Great Crystal and Sky Fortress Bahamut maps, whose two map entries name a `.cl2` and take that file's table instead, so the same pixel data can be recoloured without being reshipped.
cause: Location-map colour tables (.cl2): the CLT2 palettes some location maps draw with

phenomenon: Every model, texture, script or table the game opens by name goes through this path. A file the game has read before may come from a RAM cache; otherwise it is read from `FFXII_TZA.vbf`. There are no loose files on disk to fall back to: a name the archive does not hold logs `[FFXII_ERROR] Big file open failed` and that asset does not load. In play this shows only as load time.
cause: File path resolution: how a file name becomes bytes through the RAM file cache or the archive, the stream reader, and what lives under .dat and .bin

phenomenon: Every file the game logic asks for by kind and number, from a map's script set to a menu image, is a request in this queue. When more than 64 of them are outstanding, the code asking for the next one stops and services the queue until a slot frees up, which can lengthen a load.
cause: File requests and the read queue: the request slots, how a load is queued, sized, read in parts and completed, and how a caller waits, asks or cancels

phenomenon: Nothing directly. Every file the game loads by kind and number, from a map's script to a menu image, is sized from this table before it is read; a file the table marks absent is never read, and a missing or short table stops the game at start-up.
cause: File size tables: the per-language .fst that sizes every file by resource kind and id

phenomenon: The Clan Primer's Traveler's Tips and Bestiary pages list entries under section captions. Opening an entry shows its text, one line or page at a time, and for the Bestiary a picture page, the monster's name, its kill count and the lore lines unlocked so far. Every name, caption, line of text, picture and unlock condition comes from the files on this page. Four more families, `story`, `world`, `person` and `knowledge`, ship complete but no category opens them (Clan Primer).
cause: Handbook files: the hctg, hchk, hdat and himg files behind Clan Primer entries, how each is read, and what each field shows

phenomenon: The location map (Display Map) and the map overlay show the current sub-location as a set of drawn zone pictures, with markers for the exits to other places, lines joining the zones and icons, each zone drawn through the record of which parts of it the party has explored.
cause: Map menu files: the sloc picture files and the amap, cmap, gmap, lmap and wmap tables behind the location map and the World Map

phenomenon: Exit markers show their destination's name, or "???" while locked.
cause: Map menu files: the sloc picture files and the amap, cmap, gmap, lmap and wmap tables behind the location map and the World Map

phenomenon: A line of guide text tells the player where the story leads next.
cause: Map menu files: the sloc picture files and the amap, cmap, gmap, lmap and wmap tables behind the location map and the World Map

phenomenon: The World Map shows the regions and areas of Ivalice, the routes between areas, an area picture, and, when the map is opened to choose a destination, the Strahl's landing points.
cause: Map menu files: the sloc picture files and the amap, cmap, gmap, lmap and wmap tables behind the location map and the World Map

phenomenon: The fixed layout of the title screen, the game-over screen, save and load, the shops, the Clan Primer and its hunt list, the location map and the World Map menu. Each of those screens loads one `.mrp` file that places its frames, icons, captions and gauges, cut from texture atlases loaded beside it. Editing the file moves or recolours those pieces without touching code.
cause: Menu resource packages (.mrp): the twelve menu layout files, who loads each one and how a request becomes a relocated list file

phenomenon: Shorter loading. At start-up, on entering a map and before an event, a background worker reads the next scene's files into the RAM file cache while the game is idle, so they are in memory when the scene asks for them. Separately, every character, weapon, monster, map and font in the remastered art is assembled from a `.ah` list of its parts; a part the list does not name is never loaded. The few menu textures that are not part of a picture, such as the target lines, come from one more list.
cause: Prefetch and asset-header manifests: the text lists that preload files into the file cache, and the .ah lists that name the parts of a model, map or font

phenomenon: On the Clan Primer's Hunts page each accepted or finished hunt has a row: a picture of the mark, the hunt's name and a line naming the petitioner and the town, such as "Tomaj (Rabanastre)". The picture changes once the mark is defeated. Opening a hunt shows its record, which grows as the hunt goes on: the bill, the accepted hunt and where the mark is, its defeat, the report. The map screens mark where to go next for the selected hunt and label the place with a name, such as the petitioner's at the tavern or the mark's where it roams.
cause: Quest menu files: the menuquest list, petitioner strings and per-group detail tables, how they are read, and what each field shows

phenomenon: Nothing while it works. Loaded models, effects and tables live in a handful of large memory arenas that the game compacts as it goes, moving blocks to close gaps; a block whose header has been overwritten makes the game write a memory dump and quit.
cause: Resource arenas and relocation: the fifteen memory arenas, block headers, handles, the movable-block tree, compaction, and how moved effect data is repaired

phenomenon: Models, motions and effects appear once their data has loaded and vanish cleanly when the scene that loaded them is unloaded. An event script that loads an animation set waits while its read is armed or in flight, plays it, and frees it. The wait also ends when the read was held back or could not be set up, so its end alone does not mean the set loaded (Script motion slots).
cause: Resource lifecycle: a loaded block from its request to the free, with registration, borrowing, moves and disposal

phenomenon: Character motions, effects and script-loaded animation sets appear when their data has loaded and vanish cleanly when the scene that loaded them is unloaded. An event script that calls `motionread` waits in `motionreadsync` while the motion record is armed or its read is in flight, plays the animation set, and frees it with `motiondispose`. The wait also ends when the read was held back or could not be set up, so its end alone does not mean the set loaded (Script motion slots).
cause: Resource ownership and disposal: who owns a loaded source, copy or borrow, effect tickets and contexts, the script motion slots, borrowed views, and the order things are torn down

phenomenon: Nothing directly, but every loaded thing, from a zone's script to a model's mesh or a sound bank, is reached as a named section inside a larger resource. A hand-edited resource whose section names or offsets are off is not found, and whatever needed it does not appear.
cause: Resource sections: how a section inside a loaded resource is found by tag and name, the @FRP container, resource entries and their two storage modes, and the banked resource tables

phenomenon: The footstep sound for each kind of ground, and a second set of footstep sounds on twelve surfaces in the weather states that switch it on.
cause: Small .bin tables: footstep sounds, controller vibration, battle window sizes, the button legend, quest window texts and summon colours

phenomenon: Controller rumble when an event script asks for it.
cause: Small .bin tables: footstep sounds, controller vibration, battle window sizes, the button legend, quest window texts and summon colours

phenomenon: The width and number of visible rows of the battle command lists.
cause: Small .bin tables: footstep sounds, controller vibration, battle window sizes, the button legend, quest window texts and summon colours

phenomenon: The strip of button prompts at the bottom of menus, pairing each button with what it does there.
cause: Small .bin tables: footstep sounds, controller vibration, battle window sizes, the button legend, quest window texts and summon colours

phenomenon: The message in the quest result window that scripts open.
cause: Small .bin tables: footstep sounds, controller vibration, battle window sizes, the button legend, quest window texts and summon colours

phenomenon: The colour shift and full-screen tint while a summon's effect is active.
cause: Small .bin tables: footstep sounds, controller vibration, battle window sizes, the button legend, quest window texts and summon colours

phenomenon: The health warning and the Square Enix logo at start-up are TGA images. The full-motion movies are WebM files. Per-map render choices, which effects get soft particles, the remaster's lighting and camera tuning for each map and cutscene, the menu font colours and the screen layout come from CSV and JSON tables. A handful of files are leftovers of the PlayStation 2 disc: a memory-card icon pair, the disc's boot descriptor and six C headers. The game reads the icon pair, holds a path to the boot descriptor, and names none of the headers.
cause: Standard file formats: the TGA, CSV, JSON, WebM, C-header and PS2 icon files the game ships, and which of them it reads

phenomenon: Flickering fire, moving tree shade, flapping tents and shimmering reflections on a map are pictures flipped in sequence, not moving geometry. Each `.ta` file names one such texture and its frames; a map without its list keeps drawing the still picture.
cause: Texture animation lists: the .ta files that list a map texture's animation frames, how they are read and bound, and what drives the frame

phenomenon: The menu screens' flat pictures: backdrops, frames, the map screens' location art and line texture, the handbook and licence pictures. Separately, the font pack, the handbook pages and the map guide carry 4-bit glyph sheets (pictures of pre-rendered text) that are put into a shared image area holding a fixed number of them at once.
cause: TIM2 images: the PS2-era .tm2 picture format, how the game reads one, and the seven-slot image registry

phenomenon: The fixed parts of the menu screens: the title screen and its menu, save and load, the game-over screen, shops, the quest and Clan Primer screens, location titles and the world-map menu. Every frame piece, icon, caption, gauge and grid of cells on those screens is an item in an authored list that places a picture cut from a texture atlas, a line of text from the string tables, a bar, or a child panel at a fixed position. Changing a list moves, recolours or removes those pieces without touching code.
cause: UI typed lists: the authored item lists menus are composed from, their nine item types, the atlas registry their sprites come from, and the one-allocation build

phenomenon: The main menu's World Map shows Ivalice as one large picture. That picture is four textures laid side by side on flat tiles, and the tiles come from this file. The same file also holds a second, finer mesh that the World Map draws with a soft shading texture, and that the license board screen draws again without a texture.
cause: World map mesh (.mg): the world-map geometry file, its layout and how the map screen loads and draws it

phenomenon: The high-detail models of the main characters and a few NPCs bend some bones on top of whatever motion is playing: a joint follows another bone's angle through a set of keyed poses, or a face switches between posed groups under the control of the pose sequencer. In towns some of these models use a second, civilian set of tables. One high-detail body moves part of its skeleton with a partner model's bones, and some models are swapped for others as the story advances.

Every character the player sees moving is a skeleton of bones driven by one motion at a time: the walk or run the locomotion query picks from the character's speed and turn, the attack or hit motion an event asks for, and the short cross-fade between two of them. Something attached to a bone, such as a weapon or the high-detail body a story scene swaps in for a party member, follows that bone. This page describes the objects behind that: the player object that holds the motion, the bone records it writes, and the links between skeletons.
cause: Animation playback: the player object, track pairing by bone id, the sampler, the skeleton node records, chunk links and the locomotion query

phenomenon: As a character's motion plays, small commands authored in the motion data fire at set points: footstep sounds and dust, character sounds, weapon trails switching on and off, a weapon moving between hand and sheath, a sway or a rotator speeding up, and the character's shadow sliding, turning, stretching and fading over a number of frames. These commands are all run by the code on this page.
cause: Authored presentation commands: the command handlers and their ramp channels

phenomenon: A swung weapon leaves a short coloured ribbon that follows the blade and fades toward its tail. A few summons and one monster have trails on other bones. A trail fades in over two frames when a scene's command turns it on and fades out over five when it turns off, and it fades with its character.
cause: Bone trails: the ribbon trails drawn behind weapon bones, from the model descriptor to the triangle strip

phenomenon: A character's model can carry an effect of its own, authored into the model's `@FEF` section. It plays with the model, advances only while the character is processed, is drawn only while the character's presentation pass allows it, and can be told by a script to start one of up to ten authored cues; the cue starts the next time the game passes over the render records that have changed. When the character's record is torn down, the effect's instance ends with it.
cause: Character effects: the ticket and instance-handle tables, the stamped ids, the trigger states and the deferred trigger write

phenomenon: A character does not have one opacity. Its render record carries ten fade channels, and what is drawn is a product of several of them, so separate effects never fight: a character at the edge of view distance fades in over a band instead of popping, and is gone in one frame when culled;
cause: Character fades: the ten fade channels, their owners and the coast-down latch

phenomenon: A character does not have one opacity. Its render record carries ten fade channels, and what is drawn is a product of several of them, so separate effects never fight: when the camera moves inside a character, that character fades out over three frames and back in over three when the camera leaves;
cause: Character fades: the ten fade channels, their owners and the coast-down latch

phenomenon: A character does not have one opacity. Its render record carries ten fade channels, and what is drawn is a product of several of them, so separate effects never fight: a weapon or other attached piece can be hidden at once or over five frames, and always takes on its owner's fade;
cause: Character fades: the ten fade channels, their owners and the coast-down latch

phenomenon: A character does not have one opacity. Its render record carries ten fade channels, and what is drawn is a product of several of them, so separate effects never fight: the actors a time stop removes fade out and back in;
cause: Character fades: the ten fade channels, their owners and the coast-down latch

phenomenon: A character does not have one opacity. Its render record carries ten fade channels, and what is drawn is a product of several of them, so separate effects never fight: Invisibility holds a character at a low opacity;
cause: Character fades: the ten fade channels, their owners and the coast-down latch

phenomenon: A character does not have one opacity. Its render record carries ten fade channels, and what is drawn is a product of several of them, so separate effects never fight: the script verb `rgbatrans` recolours and fades an actor over a number of frames.
cause: Character fades: the ten fade channels, their owners and the coast-down latch

phenomenon: Every character is lit on its own. A light can be meant for one character only (a status tint), for everyone but one character, for a group of characters, or anchored to the camera so it always falls from the viewer's side. Ambient light is a contest: the highest-priority ambient wins, unless the winner is of the additive sort, in which case the character gets the sum of the additive ambients. The shader receives at most six directional lights. Each character also has a shadow whose strength fades with the distance from the camera, and scripts can fix that strength or the shadow's alpha.
cause: How a character is lit: the light inputs, the shadow casters and the shadow pool

phenomenon: A character on screen is two things: a render record that decides what it looks like this frame (character render records), and a CharacterRenderObject that turns that into draw calls. The object holds the character's shader parameters: its six lights and ambient, its fog colour, its refraction, its shadow settings, its bone matrices and the PS2-style z-bias and projection matrices the shaders were written around. A model can exist before its object is ready; until setup ends the object draws nothing.
cause: CharacterRenderObject: the per-character draw object, its model instances, shader bindings and the transform publish

phenomenon: Every character model on screen, from the party to an NPC, a monster, a summon or a weapon attached to a hand, is drawn from one render record. There are 160 of them, allocated once at start-up; a request for a record past the 160th is refused. The record is where a character's look is kept between frames: which motion event it is playing, how faded it is, its shadows and its colour. When a scene adds a character, its record waits one update on a pending list before it is drawn.
cause: Character render records: the record array, the pool lifecycle, parents and attachment, and render events

phenomenon: A talking character flaps its mouth, nods and shakes its head; scripts switch these on and off around message windows, and a third of the script corpus does so.
cause: Character rig and look: the seventeen procedural controllers, the staged look command and the focus point

phenomenon: Heads turn toward a point or a person over a number of frames and relax back; eyes move on their own.
cause: Character rig and look: the seventeen procedural controllers, the staged look command and the focus point

phenomenon: A Confused character sways, and stops while it is also Asleep; an Immobilized character has its own motion; a Floating character bobs up and down and settles when Float ends.
cause: Character rig and look: the seventeen procedural controllers, the staged look command and the focus point

phenomenon: A character hit without dying is shoved for eight frames.
cause: Character rig and look: the seventeen procedural controllers, the staged look command and the focus point

phenomenon: Monsters and summons can have bones that spin at a speed that ramps up or down.
cause: Character rig and look: the seventeen procedural controllers, the staged look command and the focus point

phenomenon: When another character or the camera aims at a character, it aims at a point the model places, which slides instead of jumping when its source changes.
cause: Character rig and look: the seventeen procedural controllers, the staged look command and the focus point

phenomenon: A character with several ailments shows one colour look at a time, by a fixed order: Stone, Petrify, Berserk, Doom, Blind, Poison, Silence, Sap, Oil, Disable, Disease, HP Critical. Curing the top one brings up the next.

phenomenon: Poison, Silence, Sap, Disable and Disease share one look, a pulsing darkening that pulls green down most. Blind is a plain pulsing darkening and Oil a much deeper one.
cause: Character status visuals: how a status changes a character's colour, light, opacity and shadow

phenomenon: A look must finish leaving before the next one appears. Blind, the shared look, Oil and Berserk fade in and out over ten frames.
cause: Character status visuals: how a status changes a character's colour, light, opacity and shadow

phenomenon: The other looks keep their own timing: Stone appears and goes at once, Petrify arrives and leaves over six frames (and goes at once when Stone replaces it), Doom has its own faster glow and flash, and HP Critical leaves only at the end of its beat.

cause: Character status visuals: how a status changes a character's colour, light, opacity and shadow

phenomenon: Doom glows a dull red and flashes each time its count ticks; Petrify looks like Stone with a dip of the light on each tick; HP Critical flashes red once a second; Berserk turns red and dark on the side facing the camera.
cause: Character status visuals: how a status changes a character's colour, light, opacity and shadow

phenomenon: Invisible makes a character see-through, and an enemy more so than a party member. Slow and Immobilize colour the character's shadow orange-red and red. These show alongside a colour look.
cause: Character status visuals: how a status changes a character's colour, light, opacity and shadow

phenomenon: Sleep, Confuse, Immobilize and Float also move the body (Character rig and look).
cause: Character status visuals: how a status changes a character's colour, light, opacity and shadow

phenomenon: Reverse, Lure, Protect, Shell, Haste, Bravery, Faith, Reflect, Regen and Libra change nothing on the body through this mechanism; KO, Bubble and X-Zone only set a flag.
cause: Character status visuals: how a status changes a character's colour, light, opacity and shadow

phenomenon: While a script or a menu turns the status display off (`setstatuserrordispdenystatus` and its `_by_menu` form), and in towns, the colour looks and the Invisible fade are hidden; while one turns on `setstatuserrorctrldenystatus`, the looks hold still.
cause: Character status visuals: how a status changes a character's colour, light, opacity and shadow

phenomenon: An effect piece follows the point it is anchored to: a bone of the character that cast it, a point on its target, or a fixed spot in the world.
cause: Effect anchors and targets: the target and anchor queries, target slots, and reading and renaming an owner or target

phenomenon: Effects are drawn in six passes at fixed points of the frame, so some effects sit behind characters and others in front of the menu.
cause: Effect drawing: the six display layers, drawing a group and an element, soft particles and the draw list

phenomenon: A spell effect is a crowd of small pieces: sparks, streaks, sprites, rings, meshes, lights. Each piece is an element. Elements are born in bursts at set intervals, move and change colour as their authored tracks say, spawn further pieces while they live or as they die, and disappear when their lifetime runs out or they leave their visibility window.
cause: Effect element runtime: instances, emitters and elements, the per-step update, birth, release, child spawns and timeline tracks

phenomenon: Each piece of an effect has a type that decides what it is: a dot of light, a streak, an animated sprite, a textured ring or dome, a model mesh, a trail of sprites, or something that draws nothing itself but changes the scene, such as a light on the characters or a colour change on chosen characters. The type is authored in the effect file, one byte per element definition.
cause: Effect element types: the handlers of every element type, what the verified types draw or change, and the kind-0x54 mesh record

phenomenon: Before an effect can play, its file is read from the archive. Battle effects are read into a small set of slots, and other effects into a queue of loaded files that are kept while something uses them.
cause: Effect file loading: the battle effect slots, the loaded-file queue, filing, sharing and releasing, and the battle effect program's state

phenomenon: Every spell, summon, Quickening, hit flash, event effect and map effect (falling leaves, weather particles, glowing water) is built from the data in these files. An `.efx` file is one effect stream; an `.efb` file is a map's effect bank, an effect stream plus a table saying which of its effects to start. A file the loader refuses is skipped without a message: the effect never appears.
cause: Effect files (.efx, .efb): the effect containers, their chunk streams, the record kinds and the map effect bank

phenomenon: A spell or ability effect appears when it is asked for, plays out over its frames, can loop, freezes while time is stopped, and disappears when it ends or when the party leaves the area.
cause: Effect lifecycle: from the request that names an effect to its release, and what an area change ends

phenomenon: Abilities and events play numbered effects on a character and its targets, and event scripts load and play effects of their own.
cause: Effects on actors and scripts: numbered effects on actors and the script effect slots

phenomenon: Outside cutscenes the camera trails the party leader. The right stick or the mouse swings it round and raises or lowers it, a button swings it back behind the leader, and with Camera Auto-Rotation on it drifts behind the leader while the leader runs. It slides along walls, rises over floors and props, pulls in when something comes between it and the leader, and when the target cursor picks an actor it swings over the leader's shoulder to look at that actor.
cause: Field camera: the follow camera, its stick and mouse control, wall avoidance and target framing

phenomenon: The scene brackets, sprites, coloured rectangles, screen images, generic primitives and the PS2-style effect packets are drawn by a family of small command objects named after the PS2 drawing vocabulary (`GiPolyGT4T`: Gouraud, textured, four vertices). The game thread creates them each frame; PhyreEngine's render thread later runs each one against the D3D11 primitive renderer.
cause: Gi render commands: the Gi* command family, the command arena, render blocks and the D3D11 primitive renderer

phenomenon: Nothing directly. On the PlayStation 2 the game handed each frame's Graphics Synthesizer command stream to the console's DMA hardware by writing a few registers, and waited for the hardware to take it. The remaster keeps that code: every frame still builds the GS register batch, writes the "kick" into one shared word in memory, spins until that word settles and clears its bits. The waits finish at once unless the vertical-sync thread's end-of-frame callback writes the word between two reads.
cause: Graphics thread handshake: the shared command-state word, the GS register batch and the waits around them

phenomenon: Nothing directly. The PC renderer draws at the display resolution, but a layer of the PlayStation 2 code still runs underneath it with the console's numbers: a 512 × 448 frame, a 4 MiB Graphics Synthesizer local memory of 8 KiB pages, and a texture budget computed against it. When a field's weather slot changes or a map is bound, the game recounts which of the map's textures are used more than once and gives as many of them as fit in that budget a compact slot.
cause: Legacy PS2 GS layer: the GS memory model, the map texture slot rebuild and the VU register leftovers

phenomenon: A bright light in a scene, such as the sun, can carry a flare: glow and ghost shapes that brighten as the light nears the centre of the screen. When a wall, a character or the edge of the screen hides the light, the flare fades out over a few frames instead of popping, and a flare that is set to dazzle also darkens the rest of the picture and lights the characters from the light's direction while it shows.
cause: Lens flares: the eight flare slots, the occlusion queries that measure them and the scene dimming they drive

phenomenon: Shiny map surfaces such as polished floors, metal and water reflect a picture of their surroundings, and lit surfaces pick up ambient colour from them. The pictures are cubemaps captured at a few points in each map, one set per weather slot. A surface blends the probes nearest to it, so the reflection changes as one walks from one part of a map to another.
cause: Map cubemaps: the reflection probes, cubeMapConfigs.txt and how map models pick four of them

phenomenon: Sparkles and flashes on menu screens: the effect when a license is obtained and the neighbouring squares light up on the License Board, and the effects on the statues of the Sky Pirate's Den in the Clan Primer. They appear and disappear as the player moves through the screen.
cause: Menu effects: the 64-record registry that menu screens use to spawn, place and remove effects by id

phenomenon: Some monsters, NPCs, summons and gadgets carry an effect authored into their model file. Weapons that draw, fire and reload, and treasure chests that open, play short command blocks stored in their own `.cm`. Every other motion a model plays comes from its `.ca` files: each motion is a list of bone channels with keyed values, plus a command block that runs on the motion's frames.
cause: Model effects and motion commands: @FEF and the motion entries

phenomenon: Every character, monster, NPC, summon, weapon, treasure chest and map object on screen is drawn from a `.cm` file: its skeleton, its textures and palettes, which parts it draws, how far away it switches to a simpler look, and the radii, heights and turn rates the battle code reads for it. Its motions come from `.ca` files. The grey look of a model under a status effect is not a shader: almost every palette carries a grey fourth page, and the game switches the model to it.
cause: Model files (.cm, .ca): the @FRP container and its FCP, FDM, FOR, FTE, FCT and FTR entries

phenomenon: A character appears once its model has loaded and the frame it was added in has ended. It moves and plays its motions with its weapons in hand, and vanishes when it is removed; its model data is unloaded once nothing uses it.
cause: Model lifecycle: a character model from its binding to the render record's clear

phenomenon: Hair, cloth and hanging gear keep swaying after the animation has set the pose, more strongly where the map is windy, and a caster's robes can be blown along one direction while a spell is readied. Faces blink at random intervals and open or close their eyes on cue. Neither movement is in a motion file: the sway is simulated from a section of the model's rig, and the blinking is a short authored sequence that picks a pose group and a texture patch.
cause: Model oscillators and the pose sequencer: per-model procedural motion

phenomenon: The story's pre-rendered cutscenes play as WebM videos with the voice track in the language set in the options and the sound at the music volume. A movie asked to stop either ends at once or fades its sound out over half a second first. Beside the movie paths the game still carries the PS2 seek indexes (`.mh`) of the old movie streams; nothing opens them. What each of the 40 shipped movies shows, with its length and its first subtitle line, is in `movies-contents.tsv`. The same table says, for the five ids whose `.webm` does not ship, which script function opens each.
cause: Movies: the .mh seek index and the movie player's states

phenomenon: Spell and ability effects fade out with distance: a particle, a mesh piece or a glow drawn far from the camera becomes transparent between two distances its effect file authors, and some fade by ground distance only. The same colour also fades an effect with the character it belongs to, hides it while status display is denied, and dims it while a time stop is running.
cause: Position to scalar: the distance fade colour of effect elements

phenomenon: After the world is drawn the picture goes through full-screen passes: ambient occlusion darkens creases and contact points (two different methods, with separate strengths for characters and scenery), edges are smoothed by SMAA or FXAA as the PostAA option says, bright areas bloom, out-of-focus areas blur, skin is softened by subsurface scattering, the whole image is colour-graded, and menu text gets its outline. Glare and the cinematic depth of field come from the PPFX library, driven by values each map and cutscene authors.
cause: Post-processing: the game's passes and their shader constants, the post-process command, the PPFX features and effect techniques, and the registries of named render passes

phenomenon: A character's motion stream is played by its presentation entries: each picks the track to play, such as the walking, running or stopping gait the locomotion selector chooses, or a track chosen by which way the character faces, and advances it every frame.
cause: Presentation entries: the reference container, how an entry picks its track, the choice selectors and the per-entry update

phenomenon: The picture is built in layers: opaque characters and maps, ambient occlusion, water and its refraction, subsurface scattering, post-processing, the PS2-style depth of field, a Gaussian filter, video and the scene brackets. Each layer is a small job object the frame creates, files in a list and runs later; the next frame creates them again.
cause: Render command list: the per-frame command objects, the two lists that hold them and the walks that run them

phenomenon: How each place and each cutscene looks after the geometry is drawn, its shadow softness, ambient occlusion strength, glare, depth of field, water and eye shine, comes from per-map and per-cutscene value files, read when the map or scene loads, and from a small set of post-process shader files. Some values in those files are left over from the tool that wrote them and change nothing.
cause: Render parameters and shader assets: the post-process shader files and the scene-parameter documents

phenomenon: The screen going to black or white between areas, around a cutscene and around a pre-rendered movie, and coming back. A fade to the colour stays on screen until something fades back in. A skipped cutscene cuts to black at once. Every pre-rendered movie that ships with a schedule row opens and closes with its own authored fade, some of them to white.
cause: Screen fades: the seven fade layers, the fade verbs and the per-movie fade schedule

phenomenon: On a window or screen of 16:9 or narrower the game shows a 16:9 picture, which the engine calls Normal Mode. On a wider display it switches to Super Wide Mode: the 3D scene widens to the real shape of the display, while full-screen overlays keep 16:9 proportions in the middle. The widest shape the game describes is 48:9 (16:3); past that the width it uses is clamped. The mode name the developer display prints is "Super Wide Mode" or "Normal Mode".
cause: Screen mode and aspect: the aspect fit, the Super Wide bound and the display object

phenomenon: When a chest or a reward shows the "obtained" message, the picture behind the window settles into a still frame over fifteen frames and comes back the same way after the window closes. phenomenon: The directed camera of a cutscene, or of a field moment such as a door opening, flies authored shots and then hands control back to the ordinary behind camera, either at once or with an eased swing back. While a shot plays it outranks the follow camera; when the last shot stops, the camera below it takes over. A skipped scene lands each running shot on its final pose. An effect file can carry its own camera, which wins for exactly the frames on which the effect submits it. The Screen Shake option silences one shake source outside scripted events; scripted shakes still play.
cause: Scripted camera: the shot channels, the camera record stack, and how a camera reaches the renderer

phenomenon: Menu pictures, icons, gauges, coloured panels and the soft-edged dark windows behind menu text are flat quads.
