phenomenon: When a character attacks, it steps in and swings round to face what it is hitting; when it dodges, it slides. None of it is walking or baked into the bone motion. An animation asks for it with one authored command that names a profile, a hit asks for the knockback slide the same way, and the actor update carries it out frame by frame, adding a small clamped step and a small turn toward the target along curves stored in the character's own animation container. A lunge covers the same share of the gap whatever the gap is, and a swing closes the angle and stops when it is closed.
cause: Animation-driven movement: how an authored animation command steps and turns a character toward its target

phenomenon: A unit closing on its target slows into place rather than halting, and creeps the last fraction rather than snapping onto it. Big reversals swing round fast and then visibly ease as the unit lines up; small course corrections produce no turn at all, so units in battle drift and strafe rather than aim exactly where they walk. Two units never settle on the same spot: each keeps a spacing from the other and tests its next step against every moving body before taking it.
cause: Battle locomotion: how a combat unit picks its step and heading, the turn limiter, spacing and avoidance, detour and stall recovery, and the corridor probes

phenomenon: A character who walks into a wall slides along it instead of stopping dead, and one who walks into a corner is eased back out of it. Ground a gate has closed works the same way: the character slides along the line where the closed ground starts. A big monster tests a wider patch of the map around itself than a party member does, so it is held at the mouth of a passage it does not fit. Whatever stands on the ground stands at the height of the collision polygon under it. The follow camera uses the same mesh to keep from passing through walls.
cause: Collision-mesh movement: how a body is swept across the collision polygons, pushed out of walls and kept off closed edges, and the point queries on the same mesh

phenomenon: Turn a character toward something behind it and it turns the short way round. The direction, left or right, is chosen once when the new heading is set and then spent over the following frames: nine degrees a frame for a steered turn, or at the turning animation's own rate when the turn is played as an animation. Which way a character is pointing and which way it is travelling are separate numbers: a party member can back away from a foe while facing it, and a pivot looks like a pivot rather than a slide.
cause: Facing and steering: how a character turns, the steering request and its two slots, scripted moves and turns, and what resumes after a cutscene

phenomenon: A character stopping at a wall, a thrown line of sight that a pillar blocks, a sound that seems to come from the edge of a courtyard, a script trigger that fires when the party steps into a marked rectangle: underneath, a handful of small questions are being answered. Does this segment cross this shape, is this point inside it, where on this area is the point nearest to me. The bodies on this page are those answers. Nothing on screen names them; when one is wrong the symptom is a walker that hugs a wall it should clear or a trigger that fires a step early.
cause: Geometry primitives: the unit sphere, cylinder and box tests behind collision, the collision-mesh ray cast that uses them, and the volume clamps

phenomenon: Every character, monster and NPC moves as a sequence of small steps, each computed from a facing, a climb angle and a speed. A character the game steers toward a point above or below it aims its step at that point: part of the speed goes into the climb, so it covers less ground per frame than one steered toward a point at its own height, and the steeper the aim the less of the speed goes forward. A creature flagged as a ground mover gets the flat version instead, where the whole speed goes forward whatever the aim.
cause: Movement step: how yaw, pitch and speed become a character's per-frame displacement, when motion is flat, and how animation takes the wheel

phenomenon: Characters and foes crowding a doorway slide apart instead of standing inside one another, a frame late. A heavy body pushes a light one further, two bodies on different layers pass through each other, and an actor that stops registering with the world, because it left it, stops participating on the very next tick. Every steerable actor stands on the ground at the height the field gives it, and the cell it stands on tells the engine what kind of ground that is.
cause: Movement bodies and separation: the movement body every steerable actor carries, its placement on the field, and the tick that pushes overlapping bodies apart

phenomenon: A monster chasing you around a pillar, a party member catching up through a doorway, an enemy giving up on a target it cannot reach: all of it runs on a flat mesh of regions the area carries, joined by portals. A unit searches for a route once, keeps it while it still leads to the goal, remembers the last two goals it could not reach so it does not search for them again, and walks from portal to portal, aiming each waypoint afresh as it goes and cutting corners it no longer needs.
cause: Navigation mesh and pathfinding: the mesh in the map pack, finding a region, the route search and its waypoints, the doors a script opens, and the obstacle grid

phenomenon: Push the stick and your character walks, then runs as you push further, turning toward the direction you push relative to the camera, quickly but not instantly. Let go and they stop. A light push walks, a hard push runs, and a key on the keyboard toggles walking so the character never breaks into a run. During a conversation, a scene or a status that holds the body, the stick does nothing; while riding a chocobo it steers the chocobo at the chocobo's own speed. The other party members never respond to the stick: they follow or fight on their own.
cause: Player movement: how the left stick moves the controlled character, the walk and run bands, the camera-relative turn, and the locks that stop it

phenomenon: Nothing directly. Each area's extra motions, its sound set and its voice clips arrive in PKFL packages, and a package is how a script asks for "motion 3" or "voice 5" of the current area without knowing where in the file it lies. The `.vpc` and `.vpcjp` packages of an area are the same clips in the chosen voice language and in Japanese.
cause: PKFL packages: the per-area .mot, .snd, .vpc and .vpcjp containers, their offset and size directory, and the slot readers

cause: Party leader: switching who you control, why the others follow at once, where they walk, and when control is taken away

cause: Party members and guests: who can join, how the story adds and removes them, where a guest sits, and what a join brings

phenomenon: The party menu shows four fighting members and up to five in reserve. During a summon only the summoner and the Esper fight, on a chocobo only the rider, in a town only the leader walks, and some story scenes fix who is in the party; afterwards the party is as it was.
cause: Party slots: the nine seats, the five slot maps the game reads them through, and how a seat reaches its battle unit

phenomenon: A PhyreEngine animation is a set of channels, each steering one property of one object. Rotation, scale and translation channels of one target are combined into that target's matrix, and a rotation channel without a scale channel writes an unscaled rotation, so only a target animated by translation alone keeps the rotation and scale it already had. In the shipped game this path is used by two map models, where an animation switches one node's visibility; no character, monster or weapon cluster carries a PhyreEngine animation.
cause: Animation channel binding: how an animation curve finds its target and how rotation, scale and translation become a bone matrix

phenomenon: Everything around the game itself: the one-instance check that refuses a second copy, the window and its switches between windowed, borderless and full screen, alt-tab and minimise, the confirmation box when the window is closed, and the restart after a display change that needs one. These come from PhyreEngine's application framework (`Phyre::PFramework`), which owns the process, the window and the frame loop and calls the game through the virtual slots of its application object.
cause: PhyreEngine application framework: how the game process starts, runs its frames and shuts down

phenomenon: Nothing directly. Every list inside a loaded model, animation, material or shader, from the channels of an animation clip to the shadow splits of a light, is one of these arrays. When a `.phyre` file is loaded, its arrays can point straight into the file's data instead of owning a copy, and the top bit of the count is what tells the engine not to free that memory.
cause: Phyre arrays: the PArray and PSharray containers, their ownership bit and the generated resize, copy and set-external bodies

phenomenon: Every character, monster, weapon, map, texture, shader and font of the remastered art is drawn from `.phyre` files. When one is malformed the game does not crash and does not report it: the asset is simply missing, or a texture or model part fails to appear.
cause: PhyreEngine asset files: the .phyre cluster header, the packed namespace, the instance data and how the loader reads and fixes up a cluster

phenomenon: PhyreEngine's bitmap-font text has one user in the executable: the debug-information overlay, a block of white text with a black copy behind it that starts with `Debug Info:`. Menus, dialogue and battle messages are drawn by the game's own text code. The overlay draws only while its enable byte is set.
cause: Phyre bitmap-font text: how PBitmapFontText lays out a string from a bitmap font, builds its quads and draws it, and the debug-information overlay that uses it

phenomenon: The window the game draws into, its back buffer and depth buffer, and every texture and constant the shaders read are made by the code on this page. The swap chain is created windowed, in `R8G8B8A8_UNORM`, and the device is refused unless the adapter reaches Direct3D feature level 11.0.
cause: Phyre D3D11 device and resources: device and swap-chain creation, the texture formats, texture and buffer objects and how they are mapped, uploaded and released

phenomenon: Every model, menu and effect on screen reaches the graphics card through the eight functions on this page. A primitive type the table does not know is skipped without a draw, and a triangle fan is drawn as a strip, which gives a different shape from a fan with more than three vertices.
cause: Phyre D3D11 draws, state and buffers: the draw and dispatch calls, topology and index formats, the state translation tables, material parameters and the buffer rings behind data blocks

phenomenon: Nothing directly. An entity is PhyreEngine's container for an object placed in a scene: it owns a world matrix and a list of components. The engine uses the registry on this page to answer "which entity does this matrix, or this object, belong to", for example when a physics body reports a contact.
cause: Phyre entities and components: PEntity, its component list, the world-matrix registry and the hooks that run on loaded components

phenomenon: Nothing directly. Each model, texture, shader and scene file states which classes and fields its data was written with, and the game lines that list up with the fields the executable registers before it copies any data. Because the shipped files and the executable agree on every class and field name, every asset loads through the plain path.
cause: Phyre field schema: the class and member tables in every .phyre file and how the loader matches them to registered members

phenomenon: Nothing. The executable carries the glue that lets PhyreEngine hand its objects (cameras, nodes, animation clips, world matrices) to Lua scripts and take them back, but the shipped game never runs a Lua script, so none of this code does anything during play.
cause: PhyreEngine Lua bindings: how engine objects are pushed to and taken from Lua, the generated adapters, and what installs them

phenomenon: The camera position, the culling boxes of models, the fall-off of point and spot lights and the distances at which shadow cascades change all come from the helpers on this page. A spot light's edge softness is the gap between its inner and outer cone angles; a point light fades from full strength at its inner range to nothing at its outer range.
cause: Phyre math and camera: the matrix helpers, the renderer's camera matrices, node and bounds transforms, and the light and shadow terms

phenomenon: A PhyreEngine mesh instance is drawn by the routine on this page; 27 routines of the game draw through it, among them the bitmap-font text and the FXAA pass. It decides which shader build each part of the model uses, poses skinned models from their bone matrices, and hands each shader the colour, position, fall-off and shadow matrices of up to four lights. A part whose effect has no shader build for the current pass is not drawn.
cause: Phyre mesh-instance draws: the segment loop, the bone palette, the per-draw parameter blocks, the light and shadow parameter values and the preprocess ring buffer

phenomenon: A dynamic mesh whose modifier network names these codes is skinned to its skeleton or blended between morph targets by the CPU. The morph codes are what move a face or a shape key between its target shapes as their weights change.
cause: Phyre modifier codes: the named skinning and morph kernels of PDynamicGeometry, their registry and the weight and matrix-palette fetches

phenomenon: Nothing directly. Drawing, animation, the post-processing effects, model and mesh data, the loading of `.phyre` files and the framework's input layer are PhyreEngine code rather than the game's own; the game drives them. Every module is started once before the window opens and stopped once when the game exits, so a module that fails to start stops the game from starting.
cause: PhyreEngine modules: the engine libraries linked into the game, where their code lies and how they start and stop

phenomenon: One of the game's anti-aliasing paths runs PhyreEngine's own FXAA effect, which the game builds once inside one of its own rendering objects. The rest of PhyreEngine's post-effect library (depth of field, glow, motion blur, MLAA, SSAO, screen-space reflection and others) is linked into the executable, and no shipped file names any of its classes. The post-processing the player sees otherwise is the game's own (post-processing) and YEBIS (YEBIS post effects).
cause: Phyre post-effect classes: the PhyreEngine post-effect family the game links, which classes have bodies, and the one it runs

phenomenon: Nothing directly. Every model, texture, shader, animation and scene the game loads from a `.phyre` file becomes an object through this layer: the loader finds each class in the file by name, matches its fields to the members registered here, and builds instances from the class's default instance. A class or field the executable does not register cannot be brought in by editing assets.
cause: Phyre reflection: how PhyreEngine describes its classes at run time, registers their members and creates instances

phenomenon: Nothing. On a machine with more than one processor the engine starts one `PhyreEngineWorkerThread` per processor when the game launches and stops them when it exits. No code in the game hands them work, so they wait on a semaphore for the whole session and cost only their memory: 32 KiB of stack and 256 KiB of scratch each.
cause: Phyre thread pool: the PThreadPool the engine starts, its work-stealing worker threads and the job batches nothing submits

phenomenon: Nothing directly. Before PhyreEngine draws a mesh it picks which compiled build of the effect's shader to use: with or without skinning, with a given light set, with or without an LOD crossfade. The pick is made by eight named switches. In this build every shipped effect authors exactly one variant and an empty context-switch list, so the pick always lands on that one build; the lookup still runs on every mesh-instance draw.
cause: Shader variant selection: the eight context-switch axes and the variant key a draw uses

phenomenon: Each frame the world is drawn in named layers: the scene, ambient occlusion, water, post-processing, a PS2-style depth of field, a Gaussian filter and the visual effects. Each layer has an on/off bit, and a frame can draw the scene twice with different layers switched on. Underneath, every frame mode still starts by writing PlayStation 2 Graphics Synthesizer register settings into a command buffer.
cause: Phyre frame: from the frame tick to the drawn picture, the per-draw mask and the GS register batch

phenomenon: Nothing in the game is random in the everyday sense; every roll comes from one of a handful of generators that start from a known number and step through a fixed sequence.
cause: Random number generators: the gameplay Mersenne Twister, the shared gameplay LCG, the graphics-noise Mersenne Twister, the C runtime rand, the presentation bit-feedback generator, the emulated VU1 generator, the counter hash and the PPFX xorshift, with their constants, seeds and states

phenomenon: Two generators decide almost everything a player would call luck: Whether an attack hits, how much it does, whether a status lands, what a chest holds and whether a treasure appears at all are rolled on the first.
cause: Which roll uses which generator: combat, chests, loot, the chain, spawning, AI, movement, script verbs and presentation, what reseeds each, and what loading a save changes

phenomenon: Two generators decide almost everything a player would call luck: Loot drops, the chain coin and chain level, the chain bonus, where an enemy spawns and what level it gets, which action an AI unit picks and the random turns units make are rolled on the second.
cause: Which roll uses which generator: combat, chests, loot, the chain, spawning, AI, movement, script verbs and presentation, what reseeds each, and what loading a save changes

phenomenon: When an enemy dies, the party members fighting on the field share its EXP; party members not on the field get no EXP. Every party member who is not KO'd, turned to stone or sent to X-Zone, on the field or in reserve, receives the enemy's full LP.
cause: EXP, LP and level-ups from kills: who receives them, the formulas, the split, the doublers and the EXP table

phenomenon: Gil goes up from defeated enemies, chests, selling, quest rewards, story scripts and a character's first join, and down when buying. It never goes below 0 and stops at 99,999,999. A party member with "Enables casting of magicks with gil, rather than MP." (the Turtleshell Choker) pays for magicks in gil. A member with "Convert all license points earned to gil." (the Cat-ear Hood) turns the LP from each kill into gil. The game keeps two hidden totals, gil gained and gil spent; the first unlocks the Steam achievement Plunderer and the second Spendthrift.
cause: Gil: storage, the gil cap, every way gil changes, and the Plunderer and Spendthrift counters

phenomenon: Kill the same kind of enemy twice in a row and the chain counter goes up; kill a different kind and the chain breaks. "The same kind" means the same enemy class: one byte on the enemy, compared with the class of the previous kill, so the whole chain state is "what did I kill last".
cause: Kill chain: chain count, chain level, the chain coin and resets

phenomenon: An enemy that is KO'd, turned to Stone or sent to X-Zone pays out at once: the chain moves, the party gets EXP, LP and gil, and loot may drop where it fell. An enemy killed by another enemy pays nothing. Enemies finished off by party-applied Poison, or turned to Stone through party-applied Petrify, still pay. Every enemy defeat, paying or not, counts toward the Blood Dancer achievement (500 defeats), and each kind of monster has its own defeat count.
cause: Kill rewards: what an enemy's death triggers, when it gives nothing, and the order of chain, EXP, LP, gil, loot and counters

phenomenon: A defeated enemy has five normal drop slots and two extra drops. Each slot is a plain percentage roll; when it succeeds the slot drops one to four of its item. There is no pity timer and no accumulating luck.
cause: Loot drops: drop roll, item slots, quantities, drop tables and the chain bonus

phenomenon: When an enemy dies and its loot roll gives at least one item, a pickup appears where the enemy stood and the party collects everything in it, up to seven stacks, by walking the controlled character over it. A pickup waits one minute. For the last five seconds it blinks, faster and faster, and then it is gone. Only ten pickups can exist at once: an eleventh drop destroys the oldest one still on the ground.
cause: Loot pickups: the ten-slot pool, creation and eviction, the one-minute lifetime and blink, collection on contact, and the pickup object

phenomenon: Each level adds a fixed amount of Strength, Magick Power, Vitality and Speed that depends on the character, and an amount of raw max HP and max MP that is the same for everyone at a given level plus a small random bonus.
cause: Stat growth on level-up: HP, MP, Strength, Magick Power, Vitality and Speed per level, starting stats, and the level-up notices

phenomenon: Some verbs act at once: set a flag, give an item, move an actor to a point. Others take time: `wait` counts frames, `move` walks a character to a spot, `camerasync` holds the script until the camera finishes, `eventsync` until a scene ends. While a durative verb runs, the script that issued it stands still and everything else in the zone keeps going. Skipping a cutscene ends those waits early. This page is the machinery that gives every verb those two shapes.
cause: Native commands: the five command tables, the begin, poll and result callbacks, the phase byte, and how a durative verb waits

phenomenon: A story scene adds a guest to the party, takes a main character away, or lines up exactly the three members the plot needs; the party's shadows and detail level change for a scene; all four members strike the same pose at once. The verbs that change who is in the party wait until the engine has rebuilt the actors, which is why a scene pauses for a moment after a character joins or leaves.

phenomenon: Talking to someone hands over an item with a "Received" message; a chest gives an item or gil; a quest takes an item away; a story scene adds a character to the party or a guest joins; a prison stretch strips everyone of their gear and gives it back later. Each of those is a script verb. Every item and gil change among them ends in the same two places: the one routine that changes the inventory, or the one that stores the gil total; a character joining or leaving changes the party slots instead (see Party membership).

phenomenon: When a scene gives a character a different body or hands an actor a prop, the scene can pause a moment while the model loads. When nothing uses the model any more it is unloaded, and a later scene that names it loads it again.

phenomenon: Every door, treasure chest, townsperson, cutscene and boss script in the game is bytecode in the area's script file, run by one interpreter a little at a time each frame. When a script tells an actor to walk somewhere and wait, the interpreter stops at that instruction, hands the frame back to the game, and picks the same instruction up next frame until the walk is done. Nothing a player sees is drawn by the interpreter itself; it only decides what the engine is asked to do next.
cause: Script interpreter: the hundred opcodes, the value stack, the registers and how a script waits and resumes

phenomenon: A treasure chest stands in a fixed spot facing a fixed way, and some chests are only there some of the time. A story scene gives a character a different body, hands an actor a weapon or a prop, or attaches a puppet; the scene pauses for a moment while the model loads. Every one of these is a zone script naming a model by one number and asking the engine to bind it to an actor.

phenomenon: A door that opens on approach, a townsperson who answers the talk button, a monster that wakes when the party crosses a line, a cutscene that one director script starts on another: every scripted action is a request. Something, a script or the engine, asks an actor to run one of its functions. The actor keeps a short list of such requests, ranks them by channel, runs the most urgent, and tells the requester when it has started or finished. When two things happen at once, the channel numbers below decide which the player sees first.
cause: Script requests: how a script function is filed on an actor's channels, selected, started, waited on and retired

phenomenon: Whether a chest has been opened, which line a townsperson says next, how far a quest has come: every such fact a script remembers is a variable. Some are kept inside the save file and follow the player forever, some live only while the current area's scripts are loaded, and two shared banks are wiped on an area change or when the player leaves a group of areas. Which of those a script author chose decides what the game forgets.

phenomenon: Every door that opens, every line of dialogue, every camera move and every wait in a scene is a zone script calling a native verb: a sixteen-bit number that names one of nearly two thousand engine functions. The script pushes its arguments, names the verb, and reads back one value. This page is the plumbing between the two: how the number finds the function, how the arguments arrive and how the answer comes back. Nothing here is visible on screen, but every scripted moment passes through it.
cause: Verb dispatch: how a script's call id reaches a native handler, how arguments and results cross the value stack, and what the guards refuse

phenomenon: Some menu entries, such as Equip, Licenses, Gambits and the World Map, appear only after a certain point in the story.
cause: Story flags: the five banks of yes-or-no flags the save keeps, the story schedule some flag ids read instead, who sets and reads each, and the flags a new game starts with

phenomenon: A new game starts with a set of map flags already on.
cause: Story flags: the five banks of yes-or-no flags the save keeps, the story schedule some flag ids read instead, who sets and reads each, and the flags a new game starts with

phenomenon: In normal play the story moves forward one scene at a time: the zone scripts start most scenes behind a test of the story counter, so a scene that has played is passed over, and towns, people and menus change after it.
cause: Story progress: the main story counter at the start of the save, the script variables that live in the save, and how scenes move the story on

phenomenon: The counter itself keeps no order. Each script write stores its value whatever the counter held, so a script that writes an earlier value moves the story back (How scenes move it on, below).
cause: Story progress: the main story counter at the start of the save, the script variables that live in the save, and how scenes move the story on

phenomenon: Loading a save puts every scene, talk and menu back where the story stood.
cause: Story progress: the main story counter at the start of the save, the script variables that live in the save, and how scenes move the story on

phenomenon: Nothing. No object in the game is moved by rigid-body physics: characters, monsters and props are placed by animation, scripts and the game's own movement code. The Bullet library and the PhyreEngine code that would feed it are in the executable, but the physics manager they depend on is never switched on and no shipped asset declares a physics object, so no Bullet world or body is ever created.
cause: Bullet Physics: the linked rigid-body library, how PhyreEngine bodies become Bullet bodies, and why nothing is simulated

phenomenon: Nothing directly. EASTL, Electronic Arts' container library, holds much of the game's text and many of its lists, sets and maps, from JSON files read through JsonBox to sorted lookup tables. Knowing its layouts matters when reading any structure in the executable: three consecutive pointers followed by an allocator are usually one string or one vector, not four fields.
cause: EASTL strings and containers: the string, vector and tree layouts, the logging allocator and the static strings built at start-up

phenomenon: Nothing. The executable carries a complete Lua 5.2.1 interpreter, wired to PhyreEngine's script objects, but the shipped game never creates a Lua state and ships no script, so no Lua code runs. Everything scripted in the game runs on Square Enix's own script machine instead.
cause: Lua runtime: the embedded Lua 5.2.1 interpreter, its chunk loader, its standard libraries and why no script runs

phenomenon: The full-motion movies are WebM files: libwebm's `mkvparser` reads the container, libvpx decodes the VP8 picture and libvorbis the sound track. Music, voices and sound effects come from the sound banks, whose materials the sound driver decodes with the CRI HCA decoder or, for Ogg Vorbis material, with Tremor and libogg. None of these libraries is the game's own code; each is linked in whole or in part as its authors published it.
cause: Media decoder libraries: libwebm, libvpx VP8, libvorbis, Tremor, libogg and the CRI HCA decoder as the game uses them

phenomenon: The remaster's glare around bright light and its depth of field come from a bought-in post-effect library, Silicon Studio's YEBIS, whose core calls itself PPFX. The game hands it each rendered frame and it writes the finished image. The Glare and DepthofField options in the settings switch those two effects; the `EnableYebis` configuration key switches the whole pass off, and then the frame is shown without post-effects. The library also carries a licence check with an expiry message, which the shipped game never prints.
cause: YEBIS and PPFX: the post-effect library, how the game starts and drives it, its licence check and the EnableYebis switch

phenomenon: Three things take a character out of a fight until they are cured: being KO'd, being turned to Stone, and being sent to X-Zone. A character in one of those states is treated as absent: no commands, no actions, no EXP or LP, no attention from monsters.
cause: Area flags: the navimapdata.bin record for every area, the town flag, the KO, Stone and X-Zone override and the other bits

phenomenon: The screen fades to black, the next area loads, the party appears at its entrance and the screen fades back in. Nothing moves while the screen is dark, and a second jump asked for in that time is ignored.
cause: Changing areas: the steps from a jump request to the new zone running

phenomenon: A chocobo comes from a keeper or a wild chocobo. A keeper rents one for gil, each at its own price; a wild chocobo asks for one Gysahl Greens, except the one at The Shred, which asks for nothing. On the Sunlit Path an Imperial soldier lends one once the party has given him a Potion, and the Jahara keeper gives one free ride to Haulo Green from story counter 1,650 on.
cause: Chocobos and airships: riding a chocobo, the ride timer and its dismount, and aerodrome travel

phenomenon: A gate swings open and the corridor behind it can be walked. A locked door, a wall of light or a fallen pillar bars the way until a switch is pulled or the story moves on. A bridge appears, a ladder is lowered, rubble vanishes. Blocked ground stops the party at an invisible line, and the monsters and townspeople that walk the same map stop at the same line.
cause: Doors, gates and map changes: the override table the setmapid verbs write, what its floor, wall and mj bits block, the show and hide model masks and when a new map clears them

phenomenon: When the last main character still standing falls (guests do not count, and a standing reserve member opens the party screen instead), everyone on the field stops where they are, the screen dims, the music fades and the GAME OVER image appears. After a while, or as soon as a button is pressed once the image has settled, the screen fades to black and the title screen comes up. Nothing is reloaded along the way: the field, the party and everything that happened since the last save are gone, and play resumes only when the player loads a save from the title screen.
cause: Game over: what a party wipe does, the GAME OVER screen, and the return to the title map

phenomenon: Every area of the remaster is drawn with new, higher-detail models and textures, yet everything the area does still follows the original map data: gates open, banners sway, palettes cycle, and models appear and vanish with the story exactly where the PlayStation 2 version had them. Walls and floors carry normal and specular detail, many surfaces get a tiled detail texture such as sand, concrete or steel, and a handful of areas change the order in which scenery and characters are drawn.
cause: Map art: the remaster's map models, the map-art context, its per-map files and the calls the map draw makes

phenomenon: Walking into a new area loads its map pack: the area's sound bank and positional sounds, its world data (the models, their placement, the lighting and the weather-dependent look), its navigation mesh, its lights, the switch-driven objects a script controls, and the picture and coordinates the minimap uses to show where you are. An area that shares a sound bank with its neighbours loads that bank once from a second, sound-only pack. A section a pack does not carry simply supplies nothing.
cause: MPK map pack: the sections of a map file, the two packs a field loads, how the loader splits and binds them, and what each section holds

phenomenon: Walking up to a crystal only plays its touch effect.
cause: Save crystals and gate crystals: the heal, the save menu, teleporting and the two bits that switch them off

phenomenon: Some fields hide traps. Walking onto one makes it go off: the party member who stepped on it, or everyone near it, takes damage, loses MP, catches a status, loses gil, or is healed, and a line in the battle log says that someone triggered a trap. A trap that has gone off stays spent while you stay on the map. Each time the map's trap setup runs, every trap's arm chance is rolled afresh, whether or not it went off before. With Libra on a party member, the traps show as markers on the ground; without it they are invisible.
cause: Traps: how walking onto a trap fires it, the trap table, the two outcomes and their odds, and re-arming by settrapresource

phenomenon: A chest stands at a fixed spot on its map, facing a fixed way. Some chests are always there; most are there only some of the time, and whether a chest is there is decided each time the game sets the chest out. Opening a chest gives either some gil or one item, and which of these it gives is decided at the moment it is opened, not when the chest is set out.
cause: Treasure chests: where each chest stands, whether it appears and comes back, and what it holds with the odds of each content

phenomenon: Some areas are always clear, some are always raining, and some change: the Ozmone Plain between sunshine, a sky with no drawn weather and heavy rain with strong wind, the Paramina Rift between sunshine and snowstorm. The Giza Plains' Dry and Rains are not weather: they are two separate sets of maps, and the exit you take into the plains picks the set from the story and the play clock (see the Giza Plains seasons).
cause: Weather: the three weather slots of an area, the change roll on entering, the setweatherslot verb, the MWeather table, what the slot does to the sky, the map and combat, and the environment variant it selects

phenomenon: You walk into the glowing edge of an area, or a scene ends and the story moves the party somewhere else. The screen fades to black, the next area loads, the party appears at that area's entrance and the screen fades back in. While the screen is dark nothing moves and the menu cannot be opened.
cause: Zone changes: mapjump and the other jump verbs, the loading flags, the moment the new zone is ready and what names a map
